anomaly.core_job: Notice when something is unusually different
anomaly.name: Anomaly Watcher

extractor.core_job: Pull useful structured information from documents
extractor.name: Document Extractor

forecast.core_job: Predict what will be needed or happen next
forecast.name: Demand Forecaster

generator.core_job: Create new content from instructions or context
generator.name: Generator

recommender.core_job: Select things likely to be useful or appealing
recommender.name: Recommender

retriever.core_job: Find existing information relevant to a request
retriever.name: Retriever

scheduler.core_job: Allocate people, resources, routes, or time
scheduler.name: Scheduler

biases_limitations: Unusual behavior is not automatically harmful
Normal behavior changes over time
Rare legitimate cases can trigger alerts
Poor baselines can make anomaly scores misleading
anomaly_base.dex_entry: Quirkle's whole personality is "...that's weird." It learns what normal-ish behavior looks like and raises a tiny reptilian eyebrow when something wanders off-pattern. It doesn't necessarily know what happened or why. It only knows that this case deserves another look.
anomaly_base.input_data: Historical examples of normal behavior and new observations
anomaly_base.name: Quirkle
anomaly_base.output_data: Anomaly scores, alerts, or unusual-event flags

biases_limitations: Fraud patterns change as attackers adapt
Legitimate unusual purchases can look suspicious
Historical labels can reflect uneven scrutiny
Fraud datasets are often highly imbalanced
anomaly_fraud.dex_entry: Swindlisk hunts for transactions that don't smell right. A strange location, amount, or spending pattern might mean fraud, or it might mean you dared to go on vacation. Its job is usually to identify risk, not pronounce guilt.
anomaly_fraud.input_data: Transactions, account history, device information, location patterns, and customer behavior
anomaly_fraud.name: Swindlisk
anomaly_fraud.output_data: Fraud risk scores, suspicious-transaction flags, or review recommendations

biases_limitations: Failures can be too rare to model well
Different machine types have different normal behavior
Operating conditions can shift over time
Sensor failures can look like machine failures
anomaly_machine.dex_entry: Geargoyle hears the mechanical version of "that noise wasn't there yesterday." Changes in vibration, heat, or other sensor patterns can reveal trouble before equipment fails dramatically. The trick is learning the difference between dangerous weird and perfectly normal weird.
anomaly_machine.input_data: Vibration, temperature, pressure, equipment logs, and other machine sensor readings
anomaly_machine.name: Geargoyle
anomaly_machine.output_data: Abnormality scores, maintenance alerts, or failure-risk estimates

biases_limitations: Legitimate users can behave unpredictably
Attackers adapt to detection systems
High false-positive rates can overwhelm analysts
Monitoring can create privacy concerns
anomaly_network.dex_entry: Netnark is a tiny digital snitch. Strange login times, odd traffic bursts, or unusual connections make it suspicious, but Steve working from Japan at 3 a.m. is not automatically a cyberattack. Good anomaly detection tells humans what deserves investigation.
anomaly_network.input_data: Network traffic, login behavior, connection events, and system logs
anomaly_network.name: Netnark
anomaly_network.output_data: Anomaly scores, suspicious-event alerts, or threat-priority flags

biases_limitations: Patient baselines differ
Sensors can be noisy
Too many alerts can cause alarm fatigue
Unusual measurements are not always dangerous
anomaly_vitals.dex_entry: Beatling listens for the body getting out of rhythm. One unusual number may mean very little, so useful systems watch how measurements change over time and relative to context. Otherwise Beatling becomes the reptilian equivalent of a smoke detector screaming because you made toast.
anomaly_vitals.input_data: Heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, and other vital signs over time
anomaly_vitals.name: Beatling
anomaly_vitals.output_data: Anomaly scores, physiological alerts, or unusual-trend flags

biases_limitations: Performance can change with lighting
Occlusion can hide important visual information
Missing training examples can create blind spots
Models can learn visual shortcuts instead of meaningful features
False positives and false negatives are possible
detector_base.dex_entry: Seeklet spots things humans might otherwise have to find themselves. Its huge eyes turn pixels into patterns and patterns into guesses about what is there. Change the lighting, hide half an object, or show it something unlike its training data, though, and those impressive eyes can get impressively confused.
detector_base.name: Seeklet
detector_base.output_data: Labels, object locations, segmentation masks, and confidence scores

biases_limitations: New packaging can differ from training data
Subtle defects can be missed
Lighting changes can reduce performance
Poor training coverage can create blind spots
detector_defect.dex_entry: Inspectra is the picky quality-control cousin. It can check products, shelves, components, or food for things that look wrong. Give it a night shift that looks nothing like its pristine training photos, though, and suddenly the expert inspector may be staring confidently at shadows.
detector_defect.input_data: Images of products, shelves, food, or manufactured items
detector_defect.name: Inspectra
detector_defect.output_data: Product categories, defect flags, object locations, or quality assessments

biases_limitations: Performance can vary across hospitals and scanners
Underrepresented demographic groups can experience worse performance
Subtle disease patterns can be difficult to detect
Models can learn shortcuts unrelated to disease
False negatives can be especially costly
detector_disease.dex_entry: Pathogaze turns Seeklet's eyesight toward medicine. Some versions answer "Does this scan look suspicious?" while others locate or precisely outline abnormal tissue. Those are different AI tasks, and in healthcare a confident-looking mistake is still a mistake, so clinicians, validation, and explanation matter.
detector_disease.input_data: Medical images such as MRI scans, CT scans, X-rays, and pathology images
detector_disease.name: Pathogaze
detector_disease.output_data: Disease probabilities, object locations, or tissue segmentation masks

biases_limitations: Darkness can reduce detection performance
Weather can obscure visual information
Occlusion can hide people or vehicles
Distance can make small objects difficult to detect
Unusual clothing or poses can be poorly represented in training data
detector_pedestrian.dex_entry: Crowdseer doesn't just ask whether a person exists somewhere in an image. It has to find where they are. Rain, darkness, crowds, and the delivery truck blocking half the sidewalk all make that harder than your eyeballs would suggest.
detector_pedestrian.input_data: Camera images and video frames from streets or transportation environments
detector_pedestrian.name: Crowdseer
detector_pedestrian.output_data: Pedestrian and vehicle locations, class labels, and confidence scores

biases_limitations: Faded ink can reduce accuracy
Cursive handwriting is difficult to recognize
Damaged pages can remove information
Historical spelling and vocabulary can confuse models
extractor_archive.dex_entry: Manusqueak turns old handwriting into searchable text. The farther a document gets from today's tidy digital fonts, the more every faded flourish becomes a tiny archaeological mystery.
extractor_archive.input_data: Scanned or photographed historical documents and handwritten records
extractor_archive.name: Manusqueak

biases_limitations: Poor scans can reduce accuracy
Handwriting can be difficult to interpret
Ambiguous language can produce incorrect extraction
Missing context can change meaning
Incorrect extracted facts can appear confident
extractor_base.dex_entry: Scribbit gnaws through paperwork and stores the useful facts in its cheeks. Extracting a date, medication, or name is different from understanding an entire document, and a confidently extracted wrong fact can be more dangerous than a blank field.
extractor_base.input_data: Text documents, scanned pages, forms, or document images
extractor_base.name: Scribbit
extractor_base.output_data: Structured fields, extracted entities, or machine-readable records

biases_limitations: Poor scans can create recognition errors
Handwriting quality varies
Unusual document layouts can confuse extraction
Language and accessibility differences can reduce performance
extractor_government.dex_entry: Bureaucritter bravely enters the paperwork maze so you don't have to. It converts boxes, scans, and forms into usable fields, but one misread digit can still transform helpful automation into an entirely new bureaucratic adventure.
extractor_government.input_data: Scanned forms, PDFs, document images, and handwritten fields
extractor_government.name: Bureaucritter
extractor_government.output_data: Names, dates, addresses, application fields, and other structured records

biases_limitations: Historical records are incomplete
Historical records can reflect social and institutional bias
Public documentation does not specify the exact modeling algorithm
Detected patterns still require historical interpretation
extractor_history.dex_entry: Archivole burrows through whole archives instead of one document at a time. A Friday Institute project uses AI modeling software to help high-school history students investigate patterns across large collections of primary-source texts about redlining, patterns difficult to study one document at a time.
extractor_history.input_data: Large collections of primary-source historical texts
extractor_history.name: Archivole
extractor_history.output_data: Patterns, themes, or relationships for historical investigation

signature.source_title: Machine Learning in the History Classroom: Using Artificial Intelligence for a Student-Led Inquiry into Redlining
signature.verified_use: AI-supported pattern investigation across primary-source texts about redlining

biases_limitations: Medical abbreviations are ambiguous
Negation can reverse the meaning of a finding
Documentation styles vary across clinicians
Health data is highly sensitive
Performance can differ across demographic groups
extractor_medical.dex_entry: Clinink rummages through clinical notes for the facts humans need. "History of pneumonia," "possible pneumonia," and "no pneumonia" all contain the same tempting word, which is why context matters more than keyword hunting.
extractor_medical.input_data: Clinical notes, medical reports, and other healthcare text
extractor_medical.name: Clinink
extractor_medical.output_data: Diagnoses, medications, dates, procedures, and other structured clinical facts

biases_limitations: Published literature can contain publication bias
Terminology can be ambiguous across fields
Extraction can remove important context
Extracted information is not automatically true
extractor_research.dex_entry: Scholarat can chew through more papers than any reasonable human and drag useful facts back to the nest. Its advantage is scale, not magical truth. Anything it extracts still inherits the weaknesses of the source material.
extractor_research.input_data: Research papers, archival text, reports, and document collections
extractor_research.name: Scholarat
extractor_research.output_data: Concepts, entities, relationships, and structured facts

biases_limitations: Handwriting can be ambiguous
Scientific names can be difficult to transcribe
Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology
Transcription errors require curator review
extractor_specimen.dex_entry: Specimunk has graduated from old papers to old fish. The NC Museum of Natural Sciences holds about 1.5 million fish specimens, and UNC's Renaissance Computing Institute is working with the museum to reduce the time spent manually transferring handwritten specimen notes into electronic records using AI.
extractor_specimen.name: Specimunk
extractor_specimen.output_data: Electronic specimen records and machine-readable transcriptions

signature.source_title: Museum, UNC Use AI to Transform Handwritten Records About Fish
signature.verified_use: AI-assisted transcription of handwritten fish specimen records

biases_limitations: Sudden shocks can invalidate historical patterns
Behavior can drift over time
Poor seasonality assumptions can distort forecasts
Data leakage can make evaluation unrealistically optimistic
forecast_base.dex_entry: Forespirit peers into the future by studying the past. Trends, seasons, and context help it estimate what comes next, but it is not actually psychic. Pandemics, storms, and Beyoncé concerts remain formidable enemies of the forecasting arts.
forecast_base.input_data: Historical quantities, timestamps, seasonal patterns, and contextual variables
forecast_base.name: Forespirit
forecast_base.output_data: Future quantity estimates, forecast ranges, or predicted demand

biases_limitations: Viral events can produce unexpected demand
Cancellations can invalidate predictions
Weather can change attendance abruptly
Human behavior can shift quickly
forecast_crowd.dex_entry: Gathergeist senses an incoming swarm of humans. Venues can use forecasts to prepare staffing, food, and safety resources, but crowds remain gloriously capable of ignoring smooth mathematical curves.
forecast_crowd.input_data: Ticket sales, historical attendance, calendar information, weather, and event characteristics
forecast_crowd.name: Gathergeist

biases_limitations: Outbreaks and emergencies are difficult to predict
Historical utilization can reflect unequal access to care
Operational changes can break historical relationships
forecast_patient.dex_entry: Wardwisp tries to see a hospital rush before it arrives. Predicting patient volume can help prepare beds, staff, and supplies, but historical utilization also reflects who could and could not access care in the past.
forecast_patient.input_data: Historical patient visits, seasonal patterns, calendar information, and local conditions
forecast_patient.name: Wardwisp
forecast_patient.output_data: Expected patient volume, bed demand, or service demand

biases_limitations: New products have little historical data
Promotions can distort historical patterns
Previous stocking decisions can influence future training data
Sudden consumer trends can invalidate forecasts
forecast_stock.dex_entry: Coinjurer predicts what the shelves will need before customers arrive. Too much stock wastes money and too little means empty shelves. The fun wrinkle is that yesterday's forecast changed yesterday's inventory, which can influence the data used for tomorrow's forecast.
forecast_stock.input_data: Sales history, promotions, prices, seasonal patterns, and inventory levels
forecast_stock.name: Coinjurer
forecast_stock.output_data: Future units demanded or recommended inventory quantities

biases_limitations: Construction can rapidly change travel patterns
Special events can create unusual demand
Route changes can invalidate old patterns
Long-term travel behavior can drift
forecast_transit.dex_entry: Commutoracle sees rush hour coming. It combines old travel patterns with things like time, weather, and events to estimate future movement. Then somebody closes a road for construction and its crystal ball develops a stress rash.
forecast_transit.input_data: Ridership, traffic, weather, calendar information, and route history
forecast_transit.name: Commutoracle
forecast_transit.output_data: Future ridership, traffic volume, or station demand

biases_limitations: Generated content can contain hallucinations
Training data can contain social and cultural bias
Provenance and copyright can be difficult to determine
Outputs can vary across repeated generations
generator_base.dex_entry: Purrrompt doesn't just choose an answer. It makes something new. New, however, does not mean true. Generative AI can produce brilliant work, bland mush, or exquisitely phrased nonsense with exactly the same confidence.
generator_base.input_data: Prompts, context, reference data, or random noise
generator_base.name: Purrrompt
generator_base.output_data: Newly generated text, images, audio, or other media

biases_limitations: Generated facts can be incorrect
Official sources can be outdated
Workflow-specific details can be misunderstood
Human review remains necessary
generator_catalog.dex_entry: Catalogar is Quillcat with an actual library job. NC State Libraries used a GitHub Copilot agent powered by Claude Opus 4.6 to research and draft standardized descriptions for roughly 300 devices and 150 software titles, then had staff review the rewrites side-by-side before publication.
generator_catalog.input_data: Existing device and software catalog records, official documentation, and structured instructions
generator_catalog.name: Catalogar
generator_catalog.output_data: Standardized draft descriptions and example use cases for catalog items

signature.source_title: Refreshing Software and Technology Lending Descriptions with Agent-Based AI
signature.verified_use: Agent-assisted rewriting and standardization of technology-lending catalog descriptions

biases_limitations: Chatbots can hallucinate
Training data and prompts can introduce bias
Friendly tone can be mistaken for accuracy
Human design decisions strongly shape chatbot behavior
generator_classroom_chatbot.dex_entry: Lecturlynx lets students look behind the chatbot curtain. Friday Institute researchers worked with middle- and high-school students to create, test, and revise language-model-powered chatbots, deliberately investigating hallucination, accuracy, trust, and how human design choices shape AI behavior.
generator_classroom_chatbot.input_data: Student-defined purpose, audience, prompts, rules, knowledge boundaries, and conversation
generator_classroom_chatbot.name: Lecturlynx
generator_classroom_chatbot.output_data: Chatbot responses within the configured educational purpose

signature.source_title: 2025-2026 Catalyst Grant Symposium Features Projects that Advance AI Integration in Education
signature.verified_use: Student construction and evaluation of language-model-powered chatbots

biases_limitations: Responses can contain hallucinations
Small prompt changes can alter behavior
Retrieved information can be stale or incorrect
Fluent language can cause users to overtrust the system
generator_conversational.dex_entry: Meowlogue turns generation into a conversation. It can answer, clarify, and sometimes use tools, but a friendly voice makes it remarkably easy to forget that fluent language is not the same thing as reliable knowledge.
generator_conversational.input_data: Conversation history, user requests, contextual information, and optional external tools or sources
generator_conversational.name: Meowlogue
generator_conversational.output_data: Natural-language responses, clarifying questions, or requested actions

biases_limitations: Training data can contain bias
Provenance can be unclear
Outputs can contain visual or factual artifacts
Generated work can imitate styles found in training data
Results are sensitive to prompts
generator_creative.dex_entry: Articlaw is the flashy cousin: pictures, stories, music, and other creative media on command. A convincing generated image tells you that a model can make convincing pixels, not that the thing pictured ever existed.
generator_creative.input_data: Text prompts, image prompts, audio prompts, reference media, or creative constraints
generator_creative.name: Articlaw
generator_creative.output_data: Generated images, stories, music, audio, or other creative media

biases_limitations: Generated details can be incorrect
Source material can be outdated
Style can be inconsistent
Fluent output can encourage automation bias
generator_document.dex_entry: Quillcat is less "write me a dragon poem" and more "please rewrite these 450 terrible descriptions before I perish." It excels at repetitive drafting when humans keep ownership of factual correctness.
generator_document.input_data: Existing records, instructions, source documents, reference material, and formatting constraints
generator_document.name: Quillcat
generator_document.output_data: Draft documents, rewrites, summaries, or standardized descriptions

biases_limitations: Generated facts can be wrong
Content can be pedagogically weak
Material can be inappropriate for a learner's context
Overreliance can reduce human judgment
generator_learning.dex_entry: Learnx can draft explanations, questions, and activities faster than a teacher can open seventeen tabs. But sounding educational and actually helping someone understand are two very different achievements.
generator_learning.input_data: Learning goals, source material, learner context, and instructional prompts
generator_learning.name: Learnx
generator_learning.output_data: Explanations, questions, activities, examples, or instructional drafts

biases_limitations: Polished output can hide shallow reasoning
Generated pedagogy can be incorrect or inappropriate
Teacher expertise remains necessary for evaluation
Model suggestions can influence teacher decision-making
generator_lesson_planner.dex_entry: Planthera prowls the lesson-planning process beside the teacher. Friday Institute researchers had experienced elementary teachers use Gemini while planning phonics, fluency, and reading-comprehension lessons, studying not only the finished lesson but how teachers evaluated, revised, and rejected AI suggestions.
generator_lesson_planner.input_data: Grade level, classroom context, student performance, instructional goals, and teacher prompts
generator_lesson_planner.name: Planthera
generator_lesson_planner.output_data: Lesson ideas, instructional drafts, activities, and lesson-plan components

signature.source_title: 2025-2026 Catalyst Grant Symposium Features Projects that Advance AI Integration in Education
signature.verified_use: Generative AI-assisted elementary lesson planning research

biases_limitations: Language models can produce incorrect feedback
Learner models are incomplete representations of understanding
Over-personalization can limit productive challenge
Teacher oversight remains important
recommender_adaptive_learning.dex_entry: Mentamorph changes its feathers as the learner changes. In EcoJourneys, the Friday Institute and collaborators added language-model capability that evaluates individual and group activity and provides tailored feedback during a science problem-solving game. That's personalized AI responding while learning is happening, not merely recommending the next video.
recommender_adaptive_learning.input_data: Individual and group gameplay activity, learner responses, and learning context
recommender_adaptive_learning.name: Mentamorph
recommender_adaptive_learning.output_data: Tailored feedback and responsive adaptations to the learning experience

signature.source_title: Friday Institute, Center for Educational Informatics and EngageAI Institute Collaborate to Advance AI in Education
signature.verified_use: Adaptive feedback in the EcoJourneys learning game

biases_limitations: Generated information can be incorrect
Collection data can contain historical and cultural biases
Curatorial taste is subjective
The system has limited understanding of physical exhibition context
recommender_ai_curator.dex_entry: Muselect is Reelure with a museum key. Duke's Nasher Museum converted information about nearly 14,000 collection objects into machine-readable data for ChatGPT, which helped select artworks and create exhibition text and sequencing for an actual exhibition. The museum used the experiment to examine AI's usefulness and limitations in curatorial work.
recommender_ai_curator.input_data: Machine-readable museum collection records and curatorial prompts
recommender_ai_curator.name: Muselect
recommender_ai_curator.output_data: Selected artworks, exhibition themes, interpretive text, and installation suggestions

signature.source_title: Act as if you are a curator

biases_limitations: New users and items create cold-start problems
User feedback is often sparse
Popular items can dominate recommendations
Feedback loops can narrow exposure
Engagement is not the same as satisfaction
recommender_base.dex_entry: Suggestle studies a giant pile of choices and chirps, "THIS ONE. YOU WANT THIS ONE." Recommendations can reduce overload beautifully, but repeatedly feeding people what they already clicked can turn personalization into a very comfortable little tunnel.
recommender_base.input_data: User interactions, item information, preferences, and contextual signals
recommender_base.name: Suggestle

biases_limitations: Feedback loops can narrow exposure
Popular content can crowd out niche content
Engagement optimization can conflict with user well-being
Repeated recommendations can create filter bubbles
recommender_content.dex_entry: Reelure uses flashy plumage to tempt you toward the next song, movie, or article. The important question isn't just whether it predicts another click. It is whether more engagement is actually the outcome we wanted.
recommender_content.input_data: Viewing history, listening history, clicks, ratings, and content metadata
recommender_content.name: Reelure
recommender_content.output_data: Ranked recommendations for media, art, articles, or entertainment

biases_limitations: Performance is not the same as understanding
Learner state is only partially observable
Personalization can narrow exploration
Historical learning data can reflect unequal opportunity
recommender_learning.dex_entry: Curriquill wants to know what would help you learn next. It may offer another practice problem, a reading, or a different explanation, but students have motivations and misunderstandings that don't fit neatly into click histories.
recommender_learning.input_data: Learner history, performance, interests, activity, and available learning resources
recommender_learning.name: Curriquill
recommender_learning.output_data: Ranked learning resources or recommended next activities

biases_limitations: Sparse history limits personalization
Preferences change with context
Popularity can dominate suggestions
Allergies and medical restrictions cannot be treated as probabilistic guesses
recommender_menu.dex_entry: Nibblet flits around the menu asking, "What sounds good today?" Preference prediction is useful for taste. Allergies and medical restrictions are different. Those belong in hard safety constraints, not "the bird thinks you'll probably be fine."
recommender_menu.input_data: Past orders, stated preferences, dietary constraints, menu items, and current context
recommender_menu.name: Nibblet

biases_limitations: Popularity can dominate recommendation lists
Sparse histories make personalization difficult
Purchases are imperfect signals of preference
Recommendations can reinforce past behavior
recommender_product.dex_entry: Cartivore collects shiny products and pushes the promising ones toward you. One innocent lamp purchase may convince it that lamps are now your defining personality trait, because behavioral data is useful but not clairvoyant.
recommender_product.input_data: Product views, purchases, ratings, user behavior, and product metadata
recommender_product.name: Cartivore

biases_limitations: Corpus coverage limits what can be recommended
Citation and popularity patterns can shape results
Semantic matching can misunderstand user intent
A recommendation is not evidence that a source is trustworthy
recommender_research.dex_entry: Referaptor swoops in carrying papers you didn't know you needed. NC State Libraries offers Keenious, an AI tool that analyzes writing or a text sample and recommends relevant scholarly publications. It can uncover literature beyond obvious keywords, but you still have to decide whether the papers are good evidence.
recommender_research.input_data: User writing, thesis statements, outlines, or research topics
recommender_research.name: Referaptor

biases_limitations: Vocabulary mismatch can hide relevant results
Embeddings can reflect training-data bias
Incomplete indexes limit what can be found
Relevance is not the same as truth
retriever_base.dex_entry: Searchound's job is gloriously dog-like: go find the thing and bring it back. Modern search can compare meaning instead of exact words, but mathematically similar is still only a guess at what you actually needed.
retriever_base.input_data: Search queries and indexed documents, products, records, or other searchable items
retriever_base.name: Searchound
retriever_base.output_data: Ranked existing items or documents judged relevant to the query

biases_limitations: Documents can be stale
Organizational knowledge can be incomplete
Poor permission controls can expose restricted information
Bad retrieval can cause downstream systems to answer from the wrong source
retriever_knowledge.dex_entry: Cognicollie herds scattered institutional knowledge into one place. Policies, manuals, and reports become searchable by meaning, but if it retrieves the wrong document, the chatbot sitting behind it may produce a beautifully written answer to the wrong question.
retriever_knowledge.input_data: User questions and indexed organizational documents, policies, manuals, reports, or knowledge-base content
retriever_knowledge.name: Cognicollie

biases_limitations: Catalog metadata can be incomplete
Synonyms can be represented poorly
Ranking incentives can conflict with relevance
Sponsored results can influence ordering
retriever_product.dex_entry: Bargainbeagle can sniff out "comfortable black shoes for standing all day" without needing an exact product name. Semantic search makes shopping queries more human, but the order of results can still reflect business incentives as well as relevance.
retriever_product.input_data: Shopper queries and indexed product catalogs
retriever_product.name: Bargainbeagle
retriever_product.output_data: Ranked products that match the shopper's request

biases_limitations: Undigitized records cannot be retrieved
Poor metadata can hide relevant documents
Incomplete collections create blind spots
Finding a document does not determine its legal meaning
retriever_records.dex_entry: Dachshundex is long enough to crawl through the filing cabinet. It can find laws, permits, and public records more quickly, but finding a document that mentions your problem is very different from knowing what that document legally means.
retriever_records.input_data: User questions, search terms, and indexed laws, permits, or public records
retriever_records.name: Dachshundex
retriever_records.output_data: Ranked relevant public records, laws, permits, or government documents

biases_limitations: Database coverage limits what can be found
Publication and citation bias affect available literature
Queries can be interpreted incorrectly
Ranking bias can privilege already-prominent sources
retriever_research.dex_entry: Labraquery noses through scholarly literature using more than exact keywords. That helps when your wording differs from the papers you're looking for, but first result remains a ranking decision, not a certificate of truth.
retriever_research.input_data: Research questions, keywords, topics, and indexed scholarly literature
retriever_research.name: Labraquery
retriever_research.output_data: Ranked papers, books, or research sources

biases_limitations: Search is limited by database coverage
Proprietary systems can be difficult to inspect
Semantic models can misunderstand user intent
AI suggestions still require source verification
retriever_semantic_search.dex_entry: Semantiff understands the scent of an idea, not just its exact spelling. Duke Libraries documents academic-search tools that use AI to interpret natural-language queries, surface related concepts, and suggest relevant sources. Here AI isn't writing the scholarship. It is helping researchers find their way to it.
explainability: compare conventional and semantic search results
retriever_semantic_search.input_data: Natural-language research queries, article text, or research concepts
retriever_semantic_search.name: Semantiff
retriever_semantic_search.output_data: Structured searches, related concepts, and ranked scholarly sources

signature.verified_use: AI-assisted semantic academic search and discovery

biases_limitations: A poorly chosen objective can optimize the wrong thing
Human needs may be missing from formal constraints
Large optimization problems can be computationally difficult
Efficient solutions are not automatically fair solutions
scheduler_base.dex_entry: Plancton swims through the problem of "too many things, not enough time." Unlike a forecaster, it doesn't merely predict what might happen. It chooses a plan. That means whoever defines "best" quietly defines what Plancton will optimize for.
scheduler_base.input_data: Resources, jobs, timing constraints, operational constraints, and optimization objectives
scheduler_base.name: Plancton
scheduler_base.output_data: Assignments, schedules, routes, or resource-allocation plans

biases_limitations: Traffic changes quickly
Map data can be wrong
Unrealistic delivery windows can produce bad plans
Efficiency targets can create pressure on workers
scheduler_delivery.dex_entry: Parcelprawn answers the deceptively horrible question "Who delivers what, in what order, by which route?" A handful of stops produces a shocking number of possible plans, which is why optimization gets invited to the party.
scheduler_delivery.input_data: Orders, destinations, vehicle capacity, travel times, and delivery constraints
scheduler_delivery.name: Parcelprawn
scheduler_delivery.output_data: Delivery routes, stop sequences, and order assignments

biases_limitations: Emergencies can invalidate plans
Important human constraints can be omitted
Efficiency can conflict with fairness or access
Resource shortages can make every available solution imperfect
scheduler_hospital.dex_entry: Wardray plays very high-stakes Tetris with beds, staff, equipment, and time. A mathematically efficient schedule can still be terrible if the objective forgot something important about actual humans.
scheduler_hospital.input_data: Beds, staff availability, appointments, equipment availability, patient needs, and operational constraints
scheduler_hospital.name: Wardray

biases_limitations: Speech or language errors can create incorrect bookings
Accessibility needs can be complex
Unusual trip requests may require human help
A human or app fallback is important
scheduler_ride_booking.dex_entry: Cabcrab takes reservations after the humans clock out. GoDurham documents an AI scheduler and calling system that can help eligible riders manage or book trips outside staffed reservation hours. This is conversational AI meeting a very practical scheduling job, where accessibility and an escape hatch to humans matter enormously.
scheduler_ride_booking.input_data: Rider identity, pickup location, drop-off location, requested times, and trip details
scheduler_ride_booking.name: Cabcrab
scheduler_ride_booking.output_data: Scheduled trip details and booking confirmation

biases_limitations: Camera blind spots can hide road users
Weather can reduce visual quality

scheduler_traffic_signal.dex_entry: Signalquid glows red, yellow, and green for a reason. Raleigh's 2026 pilot uses AI to turn real-time traffic-camera video into data that transportation staff can use to improve signal timing and safety. The city says the pilot does not store video or collect identifying information.
scheduler_traffic_signal.name: Signalquid
scheduler_traffic_signal.output_data: Traffic measurements used to support signal-timing and safety decisions

signature.source_title: AI Pilot Program: Raleigh on the Move
signature.verified_use: AI analysis of traffic-camera video for traffic data and signal-timing improvement

biases_limitations: Traffic conditions are uncertain
Accessibility needs must be represented explicitly
Service efficiency can conflict with geographic equity
Small delays can cascade through a transit network
scheduler_transit.dex_entry: Routeopus has eight metaphorical arms and all of them are holding a timetable. It coordinates vehicles, routes, and timing, asking not merely "Will traffic be bad?" but "Given that, what should we do?"
scheduler_transit.input_data: Routes, vehicles, schedules, GPS positions, passenger demand, and traffic conditions
scheduler_transit.name: Routeopus
scheduler_transit.output_data: Routing, dispatch, timing, or vehicle-assignment decisions

biases_limitations: Public documentation does not specify the exact model
Priority for one vehicle can affect other road users
Benefits can vary by route and intersection
Limited deployment can make generalization difficult
scheduler_transit_flow.dex_entry: Flowfin rides the current instead of merely planning it. GoDurham has experimented with AI-powered tools that process onboard GPS, schedule, and performance information to support transit priority and reduce travel time in heavy traffic. Durham Station is the gameplay anchor for this system-level example, not a claim that the AI exists only at that coordinate.
scheduler_transit_flow.input_data: Bus GPS positions, schedule data, and on-time performance data
scheduler_transit_flow.name: Flowfin
scheduler_transit_flow.output_data: Transit-priority information or operational decisions intended to reduce travel time

signature.source_title: Durham, N.C., Looks to AI to Boost Transit Performance
signature.verified_use: AI-supported transit signal priority and performance optimization

biases_limitations: Worker preferences can be undervalued
Historical demand can reinforce chronic understaffing
Fairness across workers can conflict with efficiency
Schedule quality depends on accurate availability data
scheduler_workforce.dex_entry: Shiftshark circles the roster until every shift is covered. Good scheduling balances demand, skills, laws, and worker preferences. Bad scheduling treats humans like identical puzzle pieces.
scheduler_workforce.input_data: Demand forecasts, worker availability, worker skills, preferences, and labor rules
scheduler_workforce.name: Shiftshark
